newsitem.title: USA: US House passes mortgage insurance curtailment.
newsitem.headline: US House passes mortgage insurance curtailment.

text.p: The House of Representatives approved a bill Wednesday to curtail unneccessary mortgage insurance policies that consumer advocates say cost homeowners millions of dollars a year.
By a vote of 421 to seven, the House adopted the Homeowners Insurance Protection Act, a bill that would allow homeowners to cancel mortgage insurance when they build up sufficient equity.

"The truth is that a vast number of people are paying for insurance they no longer need," Rep Henry Gonzalez said during the debate on the bill. The Texas Democrat urged the Senate to quickly pass the measure.
Currently, mortgage lenders require a borrower to obtain and pay for such insurance when the borrower is making a relatively small down payment, such as five percent of the purchase price of a home.
Borrowers putting down 20 percent or more generally are not required to obtain mortgage insurance, which can cost $300 to $900 a year.

The bill would automatically cancel a mortgage insurance policy if the homeowner were current on mortgage payments and had built up 25 percent equity of the original value of the house. Homeowner's equity is the value of the home after subtracting the remaining amount of principal on the mortgage.
The bill would not not apply to existing mortgages. The new rules would cover only mortgages and refinancings closed a year after enactment.
The bill is also not intended to apply to insurance on pools of mortgages securitized in mortgage-backed securities, House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach of Iowa said.
Consumer advocates forecast the overwhelming vote for the bill in the House would prompt the Senate to act quickly.

"I think it would be hard for the Senate to resist moving forward," said Michelle Meier, counsel for government affairs at Consumers Union. The House vote "brings us really close to getting a final measure."

Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato said after the vote he would seek to rally support for his version of the bill. The Banking Committee has not scheduled a vote on the bill yet, however.

"I will continue to fight in the Senate to build a consensus around my legislation which provides strong and automatic cancellation provisions that protect working families," the New York Republican said in a statement. "The current (private mortgage insurance) system is a racket for a handful of highly profitable companies."
-- Aaron Pressman((202-898-8312)) Wednesday, 16 April 1997 19:10:07 ENDS nWAT3151
